newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa to close ports in corruption crackdown.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa to close ports in corruption crackdown.

text.p: South Africa will close some commercial entry points as part of a renewed crackdown on crime and corruption, President Nelson Mandela said on Friday.
Opening the third session of South Africa's first democratic parliament, Mandela warned however that "success depends on our whole society adopting a new value system."

Mandela said part of the campaign would involve closing some of the so-called international ports of entry around the country, probably the many small airports authorised to accept flights from neighbouring countries.
He said entry points established under white rule made South Africa a haven for criminals, drug smugglers and corrupt border officials and constituted a threat to national security.
South Africa has suffered a crime wave since the transition from white rule to democracy in 1994 with rising reports of murder, car hijacking and crimes against children.

"Let me warn criminals...we will make their life really difficult this year. We are closing in on them and we shall demonstrate convincingly that, in our young democracy, crime does not pay," he said.
Law and Order Minister Sydney Mufamadi and Justice Minister Dullah Omar were expected to give details of the crackdown at a news conference later on Friday.

In an apparent reference to a Christmas Eve bomb blast that killed four people in Worcester, near Cape Town, Mandela said police were convinced they had thwarted right-wing plans to undermine the country's young democracy.
"We have examined these dark clouds and we are certain that the storm they threatened to bring has been averted," he said.
He warned militant Moslem vigilantes that the government would not allow anyone to take the law into his own hands.
In an apparent reference to the Moslem group People Against Gangsterism and Drugs (Pagad), who last year publicly burned a gang leader to death, Mandela said:
"We also become our own worst enemies by cooperating with forces which commit crimes such as murder and destruction of property in the name of campaigning against gangs and drugs."
